questions.question:
Consider the problem of reversing a singly linked list. To take an example, given the linked list below,

the reversed linked list should look like

Which one of the following statements is TRUE about the time complexity of algorithms that solve the above problem in O(1) space?

options.A: The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
options.B: The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n \log n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
options.C: The best algorithm for the problem takes [latex]\theta(n^2)[/latex] time in the worst case.
options.D: It is not possible to reverse a singly linked list in O(1) space.

questions.explanation:
Walk the list once with three pointers (prev, curr, next), reversing each link as you go:
next = curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next; curr[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next.

Each node is visited once and only 3 extra pointers are used, so it takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time in [latex]O(1)[/latex] space. It cannot be faster, because every link must be changed.

Answer: The best algorithm takes [latex]\theta(n)[/latex] time in the worst case

questions.question: Let H be a binary min-heap consisting of n elements implemented as an array. What is the worst case time complexity of an optimal algorithm to find the maximum element in H?
questions.explanation:
In a min-heap the maximum is in one of the [latex]\lceil n/2\rceil[/latex] leaves, and the leaves are not ordered among themselves, so all of them must be checked: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]

questions.question:
A circular queue has been implemented using a single linked list where each node consists of a value and a single pointer pointing to the next node. We maintain exactly two external pointers FRONT and REAR pointing to the front node and the rear node of the queue, respectively. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT for such a circular queue, so that insertion and deletion operation can be performed in O (1) time ?

I. Next pointer of front node points to the rear node.
II. Next pointer of rear node points to the front node.
questions.explanation:
Insert at REAR (new node after rear) and delete at FRONT. For both in [latex]O(1)[/latex], the rear node's next must point to the front node, which makes the list circular. Front's next points to the second node, not to rear.

Answer: II only

questions.question: Suppose n and p are unsigned int variables in a C program. We wish to set p to [latex]^nC_3[/latex]. If n is large, which one of the following statements is most likely to set p correctly?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)(n[latex]-[/latex]2) is computed first, which overflows for large n.
- Option 2: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)/2 is always an exact integer; multiplying by (n[latex]-[/latex]2) gives a multiple of 3, so /3 is also exact. Intermediate values stay small.
- Option 3: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)/3 need not be exact (e.g. n = 5: 20/3), so truncation gives wrong result.
- Option 4: divides by 2 and then by 6, i.e. by 12 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] wrong.

Answer: p = n * (n - 1) / 2 * (n-2) / 3;

questions.question:
Consider a hash table [latex]P[0,1, \ldots, 10][/latex] that is initially empty. The hash table is maintained using open addressing with linear probing. The hash function used is [latex]h(x)=(x+7) \bmod 11[/latex].

Consider the following sequence of insertions performed on [latex]P[/latex] :

[latex] \text { 1,13, 22, 15, 11, } 24 [/latex]

Which of the following positions in the hash table is/are empty after these insertions are performed?
questions.explanation:
Hash function: [latex]h(x)=(x+7)\bmod 11[/latex], table size [latex]11[/latex] (indices [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]10[/latex]), linear probing.

Compute initial hash and, on collision, probe the next slot(s) circularly:
[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Key}&h(x)&\text{Placed at}\\\hline 1&8&8\ (\text{empty})\\13&9&9\ (\text{empty})\\22&7&7\ (\text{empty})\\15&0&0\ (\text{empty})\\11&7&7\text{ taken}\to8\text{ taken}\to9\text{ taken}\to10\ (\text{empty})\\24&9&9\text{ taken}\to10\text{ taken}\to0\text{ taken}\to1\ (\text{empty})\end{array}[/latex]

Final table: [latex]0{:}15,\ 1{:}24,\ 7{:}22,\ 8{:}1,\ 9{:}13,\ 10{:}11[/latex]. Positions [latex]2,3,4,5,6[/latex] remain empty.

Of the choices given (0, 10, 2, 1), only position 2 is empty — the others (0, 1, 10) are all occupied.

Answer: Position 2

questions.question: Let P be an array containing n integers. Let t be the lowest upper bound on the number of comparisons of the array elements, required to find the minimum and maximum values in an arbitrary array of n elements. Which one of the following choices is correct?
questions.explanation:
Process elements in pairs: compare the two, then compare the smaller with the current min and the larger with the current max. That is 3 comparisons per 2 elements: about [latex]\lceil3n/2\rceil-2[/latex] comparisons, and this is optimal.

So [latex]t \gt n[/latex] and [latex]t\le3\lceil n/2\rceil[/latex].

Answer: [latex]t \gt n[/latex] and [latex]t\le3\lceil\frac n2\rceil[/latex]

questions.question:
A meld operation on two instances of a data structure combines them into one single instance of the same data structure. Consider the following data structures:

P: Unsorted doubly linked list with pointers to the head node and tail node of the list.
Q: Min-heap implemented using an array.
R: Binary Search Tree.

Which ONE of the following options gives the worst-case time complexities for meld operation on instances of size [latex]n [/latex] of these data structures?
questions.explanation:
P (unsorted doubly linked list with head/tail pointers): meld by simply linking the tail of the first list to the head of the second, and updating the tail pointer — a constant number of pointer updates. [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex].

Q (min-heap, array-based): meld two size-[latex]n[/latex] heaps by concatenating their underlying arrays and running the standard bottom-up heap-build procedure, which is known to run in linear time. [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] (not [latex]\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], since build-heap itself is linear).

R (Binary Search Tree): convert each BST to a sorted list via an inorder traversal (linear time), merge the two sorted lists (linear time), then rebuild a balanced BST from the merged sorted list (linear time) — the whole meld is achievable in [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] overall.

Answer: P: Θ(1), Q: Θ(n), R: Θ(n)

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
Let A be an array of 31 numbers consisting of sequence of 0's followed by a sequence of 1's.
The problem is to find the smallest index i that A[i] is 1 by probing the minimum numbers of
locations in A. The worst case number of probes performed by an optimal algorithm is
_____________.
questions.explanation:
The array is sorted (0s then 1s), so binary search finds the first 1. 31 numbers give 32 possible answers (the first 1 can be at any position, or there are no 1s), which needs [latex]\log_2 32=5[/latex] probes.

Answer: 5

questions.question:
Consider a dynamic hashing approach for 4-bit integer keys:

1. There is a main hash table of size 4.
2. The 2 least significant bits of a key is used to index into the main hash table.
3. Initially, the main hash table entries are empty.
4. Thereafter, when more keys are hashed into it, to resolve collisions, the set of all keys corresponding to a main hash table. entry is organized as a binary tree that grows on demand.
5. First, the 3rd least significant bit is used to divide the keys into left and right subtrees.
6. To resolve more collisions, each node of the binary tree is further sub-divided into left and right subtrees based on the 4th least significant bit.
7. A split is done only if it is needed, i.e., only when there is a collision.

Consider the following state of the hash table.

Which of the following sequences of key insertions can cause the above state of the hash table (assume the keys are in decimal notation)?
questions.explanation:
Read the state: index 00 empty; 01 has 3 keys (one with 3rd bit 0, two with 3rd bit 1, split by the 4th bit); 10 has 2 keys (3rd bit 0 and 1); 11 has 1 key.

Option C: 10, 9, 6, 7, 5, 13
- 10 = 1010 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10, bit3 = 0; 6 = 0110 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10, bit3 = 1 True
- 9 = 1001 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 01, bit3 = 0; 5 = 0101 and 13 = 1101 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 01, bit3 = 1, split by bit4 (0 and 1) True
- 7 = 0111 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 11 True

The others fail: (A) has 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index 00; (B) has 1 and 9 colliding with bit3 = 0; (D) has 6 and 14 colliding and nothing in 11.

Answer: 10, 9, 6, 7, 5, 13
